sections.html:
The Merrimack and Concord rivers meet in Lowell, a Middlesex County city that shares the traditional county seat title with Cambridge. The 2020 census counted 115,554 residents, the fifth most populous city in the state. The city covers 14.5 square miles, and it runs on a city manager and city council form of government.

Lowell was settled in 1652, became a town in 1826 and a city in 1836. The old mill district is now Lowell National Historical Park, and mill-era housing nearby makes up many of the homes sellers own.

Eight neighborhoods divide the city, and buyers form expectations from the one your house is in.

  • The Highlands (01851): the most populated area, with almost a quarter of residents. It lies in the southwest and includes Tyler Park, Drum Hill and the UMass Lowell South Campus.
  • Centralville (01850): the northeastern section north of the Merrimack River, including Christian Hill.
  • Downtown, Belvidere, Back Central and South Lowell (01852): the southeastern sections. Belvidere is mostly residential, and the Belvidere Hill Historic District runs along Fairmount Street.
  • The Acre and Pawtucketville: the remaining two of the eight.

Smaller names such as Ayers City, Bleachery, Chapel Hill, the Grove, Oaklands and Swede Village are in use again too.

Roads include Interstate 495, U.S. Route 3, the Lowell Connector and Massachusetts Routes 3A, 38, 110, 113 and 133. The Lowell Regional Transit Authority runs local buses, and the MBTA Lowell Line has several daily trips to North Station. UMass Lowell has three campuses in the city, and Lowell General Hospital and Saints Medical Center add health care jobs, so rental demand near them can be steady.

Four installments make up the yearly bill. The Treasurer's office, at 978-674-4222, runs the calendar shown here.

EventWhen
Bills issuedJuly 1, October 1, January 1, April 1
Bills dueAugust 1, November 1, February 1, May 1 (or the first business day)
Late interest14% a year
Demand fee after May 1$30

The postmark does not count, so a check mailed on the last day is late. Only receipt by the Treasurer's office stops the interest clock; mail early or pay online.

sections.h2: If you fall behind on taxes
sections.html:
After a due date goes by, interest accrues at 14 percent a year. A $30 demand fee and demand notice follow after May 1, and unpaid real estate tax can become a lien. Escrow with a mortgage company does not remove your duty to confirm the bill was paid.

If a bill looks too high, the Assessor at 978-674-4200 can explain the value. Paying by card online adds a fee of at least 2.95 percent with a $1 minimum, while e-checks cost $0.40, which makes an e-check the cheaper route.

Back taxes are normally paid out of sale proceeds at closing, so ask for a payoff figure before choosing a date.

sections.h2: Can I challenge my Lowell assessment?
sections.html:
Yes, within a strict calendar. The abatement application must be in by the first installment date of the actual bill, generally February 1 in a quarterly-billing city.

The assessors get three months. Silence counts as a denial, and then three months remain to petition the Appellate Tax Board. The board hears your case only if every installment was paid on time, with narrow exceptions such as a tax of $5,000 or less.

Value is fixed as of the January 1 before the fiscal year, so sales of comparable homes near then make the best evidence.

Lowell averages about 56 inches of snow a season, and the heaviest season on record brought 120 inches in the winter of 2014 and 2015. That kind of load tests older roofs, porches and gutters.

If you are selling a house with a patched roof, ice damage or an old boiler, a buyer's inspector will flag it. A cash buyer will usually price those items in directly instead of asking you to fix them first.

An attorney guides the closing, and the deed is recorded at the Middlesex County registry. Your fire department must sign off on smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, and the state suggests booking that visit as soon as the closing date is known. The deed excise runs $2 for each $500 of the price; the registry can confirm the total. A mortgage payoff letter and a clear tax and water balance round out the list.

Most Massachusetts land is recorded land, filed at the Registry of Deeds with a book and page number. A smaller share is registered land, described on a Certificate of Title issued by the Land Court. Your attorney will check which system applies to your lot, since registered land follows slightly different filing steps.

After you accept, an attorney runs a title search for mortgages, liens and unpaid taxes or water charges. Each one gets a payoff letter. The fire department visit is booked, and the deed is prepared for the Middlesex County registry. At the table you sign the deed and settlement statement, your lenders and the city are paid from the proceeds, and you keep the rest.

With no bank involved, the common delays are an old lien nobody remembered or an alarm check booked too late. Ask about both on day one, and write down who is responsible for each.

Pull your latest tax bill, the water balance, a mortgage payoff statement and any leases. If the house came through an estate, bring the documents showing who may sign. Write down the unit count and the target closing date so a buyer can answer quickly. Mill-era buildings often have separate meters, so note which utilities are shared among units, and keep the boiler service records where you can find them. These small details tend to decide whether an offer arrives the same week or after a round of follow-up questions.

Owners who come to us often have an inherited house, a mill-era multi-family building that needs systems work, or a property with delinquent taxes. We make an offer on the condition as found, and you decide whether it beats listing.

Without an appraisal or loan approval to wait on, a cash sale gives you a closing date that holds more firmly. Compare the offer with what a listing would leave you after repairs, showings, open houses and the weeks of waiting for a buyer's loan to clear. If the house has tenants, mention the leases at the start so the buyer can price the timing.

faqs.q: When are Lowell real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: Bills are due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1, or the first business day of that month. They are issued July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1.

faqs.q: What is the interest rate on late Lowell property taxes?
faqs.a: Late real estate tax accrues interest at 14 percent a year. After the May 1 due date, a $30 demand fee is added, and a demand notice is mailed for any unpaid bill.

faqs.q: Is the postmark date accepted for a Lowell tax payment?
faqs.a: No. A payment counts when the Treasurer's office receives it, so mail early or pay online. Rejected online payments can take up to three business days to become available again.
Lowell is in Middlesex County, so deeds are recorded through the county Registry of Deeds. You can search a deed copy at masslandrecords.com.

faqs.q: Does Lowell require a smoke and CO certificate when selling?
faqs.a: Yes. A sale or transfer needs the fire department's compliance certificate for smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, and the department charges a fee.
